In this example I'll very briefly introduce the concept of a spline function to be used as a smoother in a linear regression. See <https://m-clark.github.io/generalized-additive-models/> for a  nice tutorial on fitting a GAM.

Instead of a random effect over time, we might want to fit a smooth spline through time. Splines are just linear combinations of basis functions and can be fit with very few changes to what we have done so far. Our current model is,

$$
\begin{align}
  \log(R_i/S_i) & =  \alpha_{s_i} + \beta_{s_i} S_i + \epsilon_i \\
  \alpha_{s} & \sim N(\alpha_0, \eta^2) \\
  \epsilon_i & \sim N(0, \sigma_{s_i}^2) \\
  s & \in \{1,\ldots,n_{s}\}.
\end{align}
$$

If we add in a spline over time, $s(t)$, then 

$$
\begin{align}
  \log(R_i/S_i) & =  \alpha_{s_i} + \beta_{s_i} S_i + s(t_i) + \epsilon_i \\
  \alpha_{s} & \sim N(\alpha_0, \eta^2) \\
  \epsilon_i & \sim N(0, \sigma_{s_i}^2) \\
  s & \in \{1,\ldots,n_{s}\}.
\end{align}
$$
We then just need to define what the function $s$ is. We will ignore too much about basis functions, but just know that they have the general form of 

$$
  s(t) = \sum_{k=1}^K b_k B_k(t),
$$
where $B_k$ is the $k$th basis function, and $b_k$ is the coefficient associated with the basis function. A B-spline is a piecewise polynomial function joined at ***knots***. 

```{r}
library(splines2)
K <- 8
knots <- seq(5, 70, length = K-1)

bsMat <- bSpline(1:75, 
                 knots = knots, 
                 degree = 3,    ## Cubic
                 periodic = FALSE, ## Change later.
                 intercept = FALSE)

## What do the basis functions look like?
plot(bsMat)
```

Lets use this to create a smooth curve.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
# Paths start at the project root via here::here(), so this code runs in the
# Positron or RStudio console and when Quarto renders from this folder.
sox <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sockeye", "SRDATA2026 1.csv"))
stock <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sockeye", "FC_StockInfo 2.csv"))
sox <- sox %>% left_join(stock, by = "PopID")
sox <- sox %>% filter(!is.na(spawners), !is.na(recruits))
sox <- sox %>% group_by(PopName) %>% mutate(sd_spawners = sd(spawners),  spawners_scaled = spawners/sd_spawners) %>% ungroup()
```


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

library(RTMB)

sox$stock <- as.numeric(factor(sox$PopName))
nstocks <- max(sox$stock)
sox <- sox %>% mutate(time = yr - min(yr) + 1)
nyears <- max(sox$time)
minyear <- min(sox$yr)
sox$logRS <- log(sox$recruits/sox$spawners)
nobs <- nrow(sox)
K <- ncol(bsMat)  ## includes boundary knots.
B <- bsMat
class(B) <- "matrix"

set.seed(1)   ## random but reproducible starting values, in a plausible range
parameters <- list(
  alpha0 = runif(1, 1, 3),
  re = rnorm(nstocks, 0, 0.1),
  logbeta = runif(nstocks, -1, 0),
  logsigma = runif(nstocks, -0.5, 0.5),
  logsigma_re = log(0.5),
  b = rep(0, K)
)

negll <- function(pars){
  
  getAll(pars, sox, warn = FALSE)
  beta <- exp(logbeta)
  
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)

  sigma <- exp(logsigma)
  sigma_re <- exp(logsigma_re)
  sigma_obs <- sigma[stock]

  alpha_stock <- re + alpha0
  ADREPORT(alpha_stock)
  
  time_effect <- drop(B %*% b)
  
  ## One line for all observations: quicker to tape than a loop over rows
  mu <- alpha_stock[stock] - beta[stock]*spawners_scaled + time_effect[time]
  ll <- sum(dnorm(re, 0, sigma_re, log = TRUE))
  ll <- ll + sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, sigma_obs, log = TRUE))
  
  REPORT(mu)
  REPORT(sigma_obs)
  REPORT(time_effect)
  
  return(-ll)
}

obj <- MakeADFun(func = negll, parameters = parameters, 
  random = "re",  silent = TRUE)
fit <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = list(eval.max = 1e4, iter.max = 1e4))
fit$message
rep <- obj$report(obj$env$last.par.best)   ## report at the best parameters found
sox$expected <- rep$mu
sox$sigma <- rep$sigma_obs
smooth_time <- rep$time_effect

plot(1:75, smooth_time, type = "l")

sox <- sox %>% 
  mutate(resid = logRS - expected) %>%
  mutate(resid_std = resid/sigma)

ggplot(data = sox, aes(x = expected, y = resid_std)) + 
  geom_point() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = 'red', linetype = 2) +
  ylab("Standardized residual")
```

This is certainly not working that great. How do we choose the number of knots etc? Instead, let's use thin plate splines and the `mgcv` package to define the basis function.

```{r}
library(mgcv)
sm <- smoothCon(
  s(time, bs = "tp", k = 10),
  data = data.frame(time = 1:75),
  absorb.cons = TRUE
)[[1]]

B <- sm$X
S <- sm$S[[1]]

matplot(
  1:75,
  B,
  type = "l",
  lty = 1,
  xlab = "time",
  ylab = "Basis function value",
  main = "Thin-plate regression spline basis functions"
)
sox$PopNamef <- factor(sox$PopName)
fit_gam <- gam(logRS ~ spawners_scaled:PopNamef + s(PopNamef, bs = "re") +
    s(time, bs = "tp", k = 10), data = sox, method = 'REML')
```

For thin plate splines, we also apply a penalty term to keep the function smooth and avoid overfitting. The penalty term, for penalty matrix $S$, with smoothing parameter $\lambda$, is added to the negative log likelihood as

$$
  -l(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbf{b}^T S \mathbf{b}.
$$

## A first attempt: estimate $\lambda$ like any other parameter

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
K <- ncol(B)

set.seed(1)
parameters <- list(
  alpha0 = runif(1, 1, 3),
  re = rnorm(nstocks, 0, 0.1),
  logbeta = runif(nstocks, -1, 0),
  logsigma = runif(nstocks, -0.5, 0.5),
  logsigma_re = log(0.5),
  b = rep(0, K),
  loglambda = 0
)

negll <- function(pars){
  
  getAll(pars, sox, warn = FALSE)
  beta <- exp(logbeta)
  lambda <- exp(loglambda)
  
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)

  sigma <- exp(logsigma)
  sigma_re <- exp(logsigma_re)
  sigma_obs <- sigma[stock]

  alpha_stock <- re + alpha0
  ADREPORT(alpha_stock)
  
  time_effect <- drop(B %*% b)
  mu <- alpha_stock[stock] - beta[stock]*spawners_scaled + time_effect[time]

  ll <- sum(dnorm(re, 0, sigma_re, log = TRUE))
  ll <- ll + sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, sigma_obs, log = TRUE))
  
  REPORT(mu)
  REPORT(sigma_obs)
  REPORT(time_effect)

  pen <- lambda/2*sum(b*drop(S %*% b))
    
  return(-ll + pen)
}

obj <- MakeADFun(func = negll, parameters = parameters, 
  random = "re",  silent = TRUE)
fit <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = list(eval.max = 1e4, iter.max = 1e4))
fit$message
exp(fit$par[["loglambda"]])   ## the estimated smoothing parameter
```

The optimizer reports convergence, but look at $\lambda$: it is zero for all practical purposes. The penalty can never be negative, so the lowest value of the objective is always found by switching the penalty off. We are back at an unpenalized curve. A smoothing parameter cannot be estimated this way.

## The smoothing parameter as a variance

The penalty has the same form as a normal distribution for the coefficients. Minus the log density of $\mathbf{b} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, (\lambda S)^{-1})$ is

$$
  \frac{\lambda}{2}\mathbf{b}^T S \mathbf{b} - \frac{1}{2}\log|\lambda S| + \text{constant}.
$$

The first term is our penalty. The second term depends on $\lambda$, and it is what was missing above: it stops $\lambda$ from running to zero. So treat the spline coefficients as **random effects** with this distribution, and the Laplace approximation lets us estimate $\lambda$ like any other variance parameter. This is what `mgcv` does when you ask for `method = "REML"` or `"ML"` (Wood 2011).

`mgcv::smooth2random()` does the bookkeeping. It rewrites the basis in two parts:

- `Xf`: the part that the penalty leaves alone (here one column, a straight line). Its coefficients are ordinary parameters.
- `Zs`: the part that is penalized, rotated so that its coefficients are independent normal random effects with a single standard deviation. A small standard deviation gives a smooth curve.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

rs <- smooth2random(sm, "", type = 2)
Xf <- rs$Xf          ## not penalized
Zs <- rs$rand[[1]]   ## penalized: coefficients are independent normal random effects
c(ncol(Xf), ncol(Zs))

set.seed(1)
parameters <- list(
  alpha0 = runif(1, 1, 3),
  re = rnorm(nstocks, 0, 0.1),
  logbeta = runif(nstocks, -1, 0),
  logsigma = runif(nstocks, -0.5, 0.5),
  logsigma_re = log(0.5),
  bf = rep(0, ncol(Xf)),
  bs = rep(0, ncol(Zs)),
  logsigma_s = 0
)

negll <- function(pars){
  
  getAll(pars, sox, warn = FALSE)
  beta <- exp(logbeta)
  
  logRS <- OBS(logRS)

  sigma <- exp(logsigma)
  sigma_re <- exp(logsigma_re)
  sigma_s <- exp(logsigma_s)
  sigma_obs <- sigma[stock]

  alpha_stock <- re + alpha0
  ADREPORT(alpha_stock)
  
  time_effect <- drop(Xf %*% bf + Zs %*% bs)
  mu <- alpha_stock[stock] - beta[stock]*spawners_scaled + time_effect[time]

  ll <- sum(dnorm(re, 0, sigma_re, log = TRUE))
  ll <- ll + sum(dnorm(bs, 0, sigma_s, log = TRUE))   ## the penalty, with the term that was missing
  ll <- ll + sum(dnorm(logRS, mu, sigma_obs, log = TRUE))
  
  REPORT(mu)
  REPORT(sigma_obs)
  REPORT(time_effect)
    
  return(-ll)
}

## The spline coefficients are now random effects too
obj <- MakeADFun(func = negll, parameters = parameters, 
  random = c("re", "bs"),  silent = TRUE)
fit <- nlminb(obj$par, obj$fn, obj$gr, control = list(eval.max = 1e4, iter.max = 1e4))
fit$message
rep <- obj$report(obj$env$last.par.best)
sox$expected <- rep$mu
sox$sigma <- rep$sigma_obs
smooth_time <- rep$time_effect

sox <- sox %>% 
  mutate(resid = logRS - expected) %>%
  mutate(resid_std = resid/sigma)

ggplot(data = sox, aes(x = expected, y = resid_std)) + 
  geom_point() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = 'red', linetype = 2) +
  ylab("Standardized residual")
```

## Compare with `mgcv`

We fitted a similar model with `gam()` above. It is not identical: `gam()` assumes one residual standard deviation for all stocks where ours has one for each stock, and it was fitted by REML. The two smooths should still tell the same story.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

gam_time <- predict(fit_gam, type = "terms", terms = "s(time)",
                    newdata = data.frame(time = 1:75, PopNamef = sox$PopNamef[1], spawners_scaled = 0))

## Each smooth is only defined up to a constant, so center both before comparing
plot(1:75, smooth_time - mean(smooth_time), type = "l", xlab = "time", ylab = "Smooth of time")
lines(1:75, gam_time - mean(gam_time), col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("RTMB", "mgcv::gam"), col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1:2)

## Effective degrees of freedom of the smooth, out of a possible 9
round(sum(fit_gam$edf[grep("s\\(time\\)", names(fit_gam$edf))]), 1)

## AIC, to compare with the AR(1) year effect of Module 5
2*fit$objective + 2*length(fit$par)
```

The penalty is doing very little here: the smooth uses nearly all of the degrees of freedom the basis allows. The year to year changes shared by the stocks are too abrupt for a smooth curve, and the AR(1) year effect in Module 5 describes them much better (compare the AIC above with the one on the "Is the Year Effect Worth It?" slide).
